Acta Materialia

Volume 58, Issue 9, May 2010, Pages 3262-3270

An analytical model for constitutional supercooling-driven grain formation and grain size prediction

Author links open overlay panelM.QianaP.CaobM.A.EastoncS.D.McDonalddD.H.StJohnd
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2010.01.052Get rights and content

Abstract

Being able to predict the grain formation process and attendant grain size has been a central topic in solidification. Such an analytical model is presented for constitutional supercooling (CS)-driven grain formation with several simplifications. The model links the nucleation of new grains to the growth of a larger neighbouring grain. The average grain size (d¯) is thus determined by two components: the minimum growth (rcs) necessary to establish sufficient CS (ΔTn) for nucleating new grains, and the spatial mean distance (a¯) to the most potent available nucleants. Both spherical and planar growth fronts are considered, covering growth curvatures from small to infinite. Two distinct fundamental approaches are used, which result in identical descriptions of d¯, where d¯=a¯+D·ΔTn/(v·Q) (D is the diffusion coefficient, v is the growth velocity, Q is the growth restriction factor). The model is compared with literature data produced under various conditions and demonstrated on aluminium alloys as an example.

Keywords

Undercooling solidification
Heterogeneous nucleation
Grain growth
Grain refining

1. Introduction

Modelling of solidification on a microstructural scale may be classified into two broad categories: probabilistic (stochastic) and deterministic (continuum). The advantage of stochastic models is their ability to predict microstructure formation in general and ease of treating complex problems of, for example, geometry or the effects of crystallographic anisotropies. In contrast, deterministic models have the merit of correlating with measurable macroscopic (or even microscopic) parameters and, consequently, are more straightforward for quantitatively predicting/validating/explaining experimental measurements. Both approaches are important means of modelling and are often used collectively because of their complementary nature in many cases [1]. For instance, in the Rappaz–Gandin model [2], the nucleation and grain selections are treated stochastically, while the growth kinetics are largely dealt with deterministically. The present authors’ expectation of modelling for grain formation and grain size prediction is that of an analytical type of deterministic descriptor which offers good fundamental insights while being straightforward for application.

A few predictive models of the deterministic nature have been developed over the years for grain formation. One such example is the Maxwell–Hellawell (M–H) model [3]. The M–H model assumes that grain nucleation occurs throughout a melt which has a uniform temperature that varies with time through the imposed cooling rate until recalescence takes place or all effective nucleants have been consumed. Fig. 1 illustrates the basis of the M–H model. Spherical growth follows nucleation until, at some stage, dendritic growth takes over, where an invariant-size approximation model [4] was used to describe the spherical growth rate. The final grain size is thus a result of competition between heterogeneous nucleation and growth. The attendant numerical results on grain formation in the Al–Ti, Al–Zr and Al–Cr systems provide in-depth information about the refining mechanisms in operation. The conceptual and theoretical treatments of the M–H model have had a significant impact on the subsequent modelling of grain formation in a solidifying alloy.

Turnbull’s transformation nucleus model [5] initiated the concept of a growth barrier for a crystal nucleus growing on a small flat substrate. Turnbull pointed out that for a nucleus to grow into a grain on a small flat substrate in an undercooled liquid metal, the substrate dimension d must be larger than 2r*, i.e., d > 2r*, where r* is the critical embryo radius. Unfortunately, Turnbull’s concept of grain formation on a small flat nucleating substrate was not appreciated until it was recently brought to attention [6], [7]. The free growth model [8], [9] came to the same grain formation criterion, d > 2r*, but explained it elegantly using a hemispherical illustration and, in addition, tested it both numerically and experimentally. The nucleus can be a spherical cap according to Volmer’s classical model [10] or a thin layer formed by absorption following Sunquist [11], who proposed the concept of a thin layer nucleus for nucleation under small undercoolings, namely for nucleation on potent substrates such as Al on TiB2 or Mg on Zr. The criterion d > 2r* immediately leads to the requirement of a minimum undercooling (ΔTmin) for grain formation on a flat substrate with a linear dimension of d by substituting the expression of r*. This gives ΔTmin = 4γSL/(ΔSv · d) (γSL is the solid–liquid interfacial energy; ΔSv is the entropy of fusion per unit volume) [8], [9]. The free growth model [8] adopted the basis of the M–H model [3], including its theoretical treatment of spherical growth. However, it differs from the M–H model in that grain initiation is no longer stochastic; instead, it occurs progressively on particles from large to small as ΔTmin ∝ 1/d. Experimental work reported on grain nucleation in aluminium alloys inoculated with TiB2 [8], [9] and magnesium alloys inoculated with SiC [12] appears to be in support of the progressive grain formation concept.

The constitutional supercooling (CS)-driven nucleation model was proposed by Winegard and Chalmers [13], who pointed out that the CS arising from solute enrichment in the liquid ahead of an advancing solid front can trigger nucleation on available substrate particles. Although Winegard and Chalmers [13] have further proposed the possibility of homogeneous nucleation at significant solute enrichment, it has been realized that the CS-driven nucleation mechanism is more important when an effective nucleant or grain refiner is present than without [14], [15]. Recent work on controlled columnar to equiaxed transition (CET) [16], via the control of the Zr nucleant sizes in the liquid ahead of the advancing columnar front in a Mg–Zn–Ca alloy, confirmed the importance of the CS-driven mechanism for grain nucleation and formation in the presence of an effective substrate.

Following the CS-driven nucleation mechanism, Easton and StJohn [17], [18] proposed a quantitative model to predict the grain size of aluminium castings inoculated with the Al–Ti–B type of master alloy. This was based on an estimate of the magnitude of CS in front of a growing interface. This magnitude was determined using the Gulliver–Scheil equation to calculate the amount of growth that had occurred. Assuming a negligible temperature gradient in the melt, they suggested that the solid fraction fsn attained when the CS (ΔTcs) reaches a critical value ΔTn can be used as a measure of the resulting relative grain size (RGS). The model is expressed as(1)RGS=fsn=1-1-ΔTnml·c01/(k-1)where c0 is the overall solute concentration, ml is the slope of the liquidus, and k is the solute partition coefficient. In the presence of potent substrates where the undercoolings are very small, the limit where ΔTn → 0 can be taken to give an estimate of the relative grain size as(2)fsn=ΔTn/Qin which Q = ml ⋅ c0 ⋅ (k − 1) is the growth restriction factor. Interestingly, experimental observations made by different researchers indicated an approximate linear relationship between the actual average grain size d and the reciprocal of Q, 1/Q [19], [20], [21], [22]. This fundamentally agrees with Eq. (2), although fsn and d are not exactly the same. Having further analysed the latent relationship between d and 1/Q, Easton and StJohn [23], [24] proposed a semi-empirical equation below for grain formation under small undercoolings:(3)d=1Nv3+b′·ΔTnQwhere Nv is the volume density of active nucleation sites, and b′ is a fitting factor.

The model was tested on the inoculation of aluminium alloys with TiB2 and produced good agreement. Also, it was incorporated into a phase-field microstructure prediction model yielding good predictions of grain size for magnesium alloys [25]. The main limitation of the initial model (Eq. (1)) is the use of equations that assume constant compositions in the liquid, such as the Gulliver–Scheil equation, which assumes complete diffusion in the liquid and therefore dismisses the development of the CS. In other words, it does not include the important kinetic factors that influence solidification processes. In addition, the model requires fitting factors to relate it to actual grain size measurements. Despite these deficiencies, it is the first analytical model that gives a reasonable description of the grain refinement phenomena in wrought and cast aluminium alloys and has been shown to be applicable to magnesium alloys [24], [26] and Ti-based alloys [27], [28] across a range of solidification rates [29], [30] and conditions [31]. Also, it forms the basis of a methodology for assessing the influence of nucleant potency and density in a melt for commercially available grain refiners or new grain refiners on trial [32].

The purpose of this work is to develop an analytical model for grain formation and grain size prediction in cast alloys, where CS has assumed a prime role in grain nucleation. The growth of the nucleated grains is first treated in a similar fashion following the M–H model [3] for spherical growth. A second approach is further presented for the growth of planar interfaces to cover growth curvatures from small to infinite. The model to be formulated is tested against the grain size data obtained from 1000 to 6000 series wrought aluminium alloys inoculated with TiB2. The significance of the model as a predictive and analytical tool for grain formation is discussed.

2. Conceptual development and model formulation

2.1. Nucleation and growth

The birth of the CS concept [33] and the formulation of its criterion between process variables and alloy parameters [34], both in 1953, represent a major milestone in the development of quantitative understanding of solidification microstructure in relation to the conditions at an advancing solidification front [35]. The model illustrated in Fig. 2 considers grain nucleation in the liquid ahead of an advancing solidification front, where effective nucleants are present, such that CS plays a prime role in grain nucleation. According to the CS-driven nucleation mechanism, nucleation will occur when the amount of CS generated, ΔTcs, reaches the undercooling required for nucleation, ΔTn, where ΔTn depends on both the chemical potency and physical geometry of the nucleants in the melt. As the transformation continues, the growth of each newly formed crystallite, in turn, will lead to further solute enrichment ahead of its growing front. Thus nucleation occurs progressively inwards as the solid–liquid (S–L) interface advances, provided that there is sufficient development of CS ahead of each growing front. Consequently, the CS-driven nucleation mechanism can be responsible for the development of the grain structure, particularly in the presence of an effective nucleant or grain refiner.

A crystallite formed by nucleation in an undercooled liquid can be assumed to be nearly spherical in the beginning. The growth of a spherical crystal in an undercooled pure liquid (without solute) was analysed by Mullins and Sekerka (M–S) [36]. A spherical crystal will continue to grow spherically until it reaches a critical size 2Rc, where Rc is proportional to the critical embryo radius r* [36]. For instance, Rc=13.67r∗ for the spherical growth of magnesium crystals [37]. The value of Rc is similar for the spherical growth of aluminium crystals. A recent examination of the principal assumptions used in the formulation of the M–S model revealed that the M–S stability criterion applies to the growth of a metal nucleus in its undercooled melt for most metals [37]. In addition, following the M–S criterion, spherical primary magnesium crystals up to 120 μm diameter have been produced in a repeatable fashion in undercooled Mg–Zn–Ca–Zr melts (30-mm-diameter samples) [37], where Zr was employed as an effective nucleant for magnesium.

Based on these considerations, a grain nucleation and formation model is proposed, which is depicted in Fig. 2a and b. The model will first deal with a spherical advancing front (small curvature). The circumstances for a planar advancing front (infinite curvature) are considered in Section 2.3.

Referring to Fig. 2a, there is first nucleation of a grain on a nucleant. The growth of this grain leads to the development of CS (ΔTcs) ahead of its advancing front. Consequently, CS-driven nucleation occurs on another nucleant i at the distance ai from the growing front when ΔTcs = ΔTn at ai. The radius rcs indicated in Fig. 2a is the minimum amount of growth needed to generate ΔTn at ai for the nucleant i; Te is the equilibrium liquidus temperature; and TL is the actual temperature gradient. The mean grain size di of the two potential grains can thus be written(4)di=ai+rcswhere the value of ai depends on the distance to the most potent available nucleant from the growing front with respect to the CS being considered. It should be noted that, because of the assumptions of potent nucleants and a strong growth restriction effect, the quantity (rcs − r*) is in general not significantly greater than r* (see Fig. 2). In other words, it is still in the early stages of solidification by the time nucleation has finished. On this basis, the model has assumed that CS-driven nucleation occurs before spherical growth gives way to dendritic growth. The assumption is generally valid under the conditions discussed.

In a real three-dimensional (3D) situation, active nucleants exist in the vicinity of a growing crystal at various distances in all radial directions, as illustrated in Fig. 2b by a sectional view. Assuming that the total number of such active nucleants in the volume considered is N, there should be formation of N grains surrounding the growing front. Accordingly, the mean particle spacing between the growing grain and each of the newly formed N grains, d¯, is given by:(5)d¯=1N∑i=1Nai+rcs=a¯+rcswhere a¯=1N∑i=1Nai, determined by both the number of the active nucleants and their distribution. In a strict sense, d¯ differs from the average grain size of the N + 1 grains being considered. However, when the resulting equiaxed grain structure is reasonably uniform, which is typical of a solidified alloy inoculated with potent substrates, d¯ will be essentially equal to the average grain size. The deviation will depend on the uniformity of the attendant equiaxed grain structure.

The chief issue to determine the average grain size d¯ now reduces to that of determining rcs.

2.2. Model formulation: spherical growth

The determination of rcs deals with the spherical growth of a crystal in an undercooled alloy melt. The invariant-size approximation model [4] employed by the M–H model [3] is still the most appropriate theoretical tool to describe such spherical growth. In the M–H model, in order to calculate the amount of latent heat released over successive time intervals of growth, Maxwell and Hellawell [3] assumed that the crystallites growing in an undercooled melt would remain spherical until at some stage they become dendritic. By further assuming immediate and continuous diffusion control, Maxwell and Hellawell [3] introduced the invariant-size approximation model [4] to describe the rate of growth of each nucleated spherical grain. This innovative theoretical treatment enabled them to quantitatively predict the grain density or grain size. The same treatment has also formed an important basis for the free growth model [8]. The M–H approach will be adopted to determine rcs for the model proposed in Fig. 2.

The invariant-size approximation model was formulated for the diffusion-controlled growth of a spherical precipitate of radius r in a solid matrix [4]. It requires that the composition profile across the precipitate–matrix interface satisfies(6)|cP-cM|≫|cI-cM|where cP is the composition of the precipitate, cI is the concentration in the matrix at the interface, and cM is the far-field composition of the alloy. Inequality (6) means that the constitutional difference between the precipitate and matrix at the interface must be sufficiently large, irrespective of cP > cI or cP < cI. In the context of solidification, this is equivalent to requiring a small value of k (the solute partition coefficient) for the case of k < 1 or a large value of k for the case of k > 1.

The restriction of inequality (6) was placed to ensure a stationary interface during growth, i.e., dr/dt ≈ 0 (the invariant-size approximation) [4], or to ensure that the radius of the growing precipitate, r(t), is at least a weak function of time. In a strict sense, this restriction is not always met for the growth of a crystal in an undercooled metallic melt. This can be inferred from the partition coefficients k(= cP/cI) of many eutectic or peritectic systems.

The growth rate of a metallic crystal (continuous growth) in an undercooled liquid generally increases with increasing undercooling ΔT [38], [39]. For a metallic melt that contains potent substrate particles such as TiB2 for Al and Zr for Mg, it has been found that the undercooling of the inoculated melt is often a small fraction of 1 K [6], [9] unless the inoculated particles are tiny, e.g., dparticle < 2r* for flat substrates [5], [8] or dparticle < 10r* for spherical substrates [40], where the negative size effect will come into play. The small undercooling implies a slow growth rate, although the solidification process may still proceed quickly because of the high nucleation rate induced by the potent nucleants. Consequently, the stationary-interface condition is approximately satisfied. In other words, the invariant-size approximation model can be applied to the growth of a crystallite in a metallic melt inoculated with potent nucleants. This inference is supported by the simulation work carried out using the stationary interface model on the Al–Ti [3], Al–Zr [3], and Al–TiB2 [9] systems, where the predictions all agreed well with experiments.

According to the stationary interface growth model [4], the radius of a diffusion-controlled growing spherical particle is given by:(7)r=λ(D·t)1/2where λ is an interfacial parameter, determined by the interface composition profiles(8)λ=-S2π1/2+S24π-S1/2in which(9)S=2(cI-cM)/(cP-cI)

For the growth of a crystallite in a metallic melt, following Maxwell and Hellawell [3], cI and cP correspond to the solute compositions in the liquid cl and the solidified solid cs at the interface, respectively. The far-field composition of the alloy cM is the bulk composition of the alloy. For consistency with the solidification literature, c0 is used to replace cM. Therefore,(10)S=-2(c0-cl)/(cs-cl)

In many practical situations of a solidifying melt, the temperature gradient is usually not significant in the bulk of the melt. To relate the solute composition to ΔTcs, referring to Fig. 2a, consider the case where TL is small or negligible compared to the effects of the solute, ml ⋅ (c0 − cl). Hence(11)ΔTcs=ml·(c0-cl)

Substituting cl into Eq. (10) by Eq. (11) and noting that k = cs/cl, Eq. (10) becomes(12)S=-2·ΔTcsml·(k-1)·(c0-ΔTcs/ml)

In the early stages of growth, when a spherical crystallite is small, it is often necessary to include the curvature undercooling ΔTr in addition to ΔTcs. However, in this model development, the principal interest is in the moment when the amount of growth has become sufficient to trigger nucleation on a nearby active nucleant. This means that, by the time nucleation occurs, the amount of growth rcs will, in general, be large enough to allow one to ignore ΔTr in relation to ΔTcs. Hence, the model will discount ΔTr. In addition, the interface undercooling due to the atomic attachment kinetics will be neglected. This is because, for a typical metal, the interface undercooling is very small, estimated to be in the order of 10−4 °C corresponding to a practically fast growth rate of 100 μm s−1 [38]. Accordingly, when ΔTcs = ΔTn, Eq. (12) gives(13)S=-2·ΔTnml·(k-1)·(c0-ΔTn/ml)

Note that ΔTn is small in the presence of an effective nucleant; |ΔTn/ml| ≪ c0 holds in most cases. Consequently,(14)S≈-2ΔTn/Q

The value of Q, where Q=mlc0(k-1), represents the freezing range on a binary phase diagram at composition kc0. For potent grain refiners, where ΔTn is small (<1 K) and where even dilute alloys have Q values at least an order of magnitude >ΔTn, |S|≪1 holds. As a result, Eq. (8) can be simplified to λ≈(-S/2π1/2)+(-S)1/2, because S2≪|S| when |S|≪1, and further to λ≈(-S)1/2, similarly because |S|≪|S| when |S|≪1. Hence(15)λ≈(-S)1/2=(2ΔTn/Q)1/2

The formulation of Eqs. (14), (15) is essential to the development of the model.

Differentiating Eq. (7) with respect to t and then substituting for t using t=r2/(λ2D) and λ using Eq. (15), one eventually obtains(16)rcs=D·ΔTnv·Qwhere v is the growth rate of the spherical grain at the moment when ΔTcs = ΔTn; v=∂r/∂t=λ2D/2r according to Eq. (7). Substituting into Eq. (5) gives(17)d¯=a¯+D·ΔTnv·Q

The growth of a grain in an undercooled metallic alloy melt is typically controlled by solute diffusion (continuous growth). For continuous growth, the growth rate is approximately proportional to the undercooling ΔT through an interface mobility parameter [38]. Although in a strict sense the undercooling ΔTn in Eq. (17) differs from the undercooling at the S–L interface of the growing spherical crystal being considered, it is presumed that they are fairly close. It follows that the term ΔTn/v may be regarded as a nearly constant property in many cases. Consequently, Eq. (17) may be written in a simpler form as(18)d¯=a¯+D·l/Qwhere l = ΔTn/v. Coincidently, this equation is similar to a recently recognized, largely empirical linear relationship between the average grain size d¯ and the parameter 1/Q [19], [20], [21], [22]. The similarities will be discussed subsequently along with a detailed assessment of the model against experimental data.

2.3. Model formulation: planar growth

As can be inferred from Fig. 2a, in the case when rcs≫ai, the spherical advancing solid–liquid interface will be essentially equivalent to a planar interface growing towards the nucleant i. Enlightened by this, a fundamentally different approach is used below to formulate the grain formation for the case when rcs≫ai, by considering a planar growth front.

The solute profile in the liquid ahead of a planar advancing front of velocity v was analysed by Kurz and Fisher [41]. In the early stages of solidification prior to the establishment of the steady state, the build-up of solute ahead of a planar S–L interface leads to the development of a transient zone (see Fig. 3) when convection does not play a significant role. For small values of k, the solute concentration in the initial transient zone is given by [41]:(19)cl∗≅c0k·1-(1-k)·exp-k·z·vDwhere v is the moving velocity of the interface, D is the solute diffusion coefficient, and z is the distance that the interface has moved from the beginning of solidification or the amount of growth [41]. Eq. (19) is valid within a characteristic length of D/(v ⋅ k), which is typically larger than the average grain size (i.e., the steady-state will rarely be reached under normal casting conditions). Similarly, the case is considered where TL is small or negligible compared with the effects of solute defined by ml ⋅ (c0 − cl). Substituting Eq. (19) into Eq. (11) gives(20)ΔTcs=ml·c0·1-1k·1-(1-k)·exp-k·z·vD

Re-arranging Eq. (20) in terms of the amount of growth z yields(21)z=-Dk·v·ln1-ΔTcsml·c0·(k-1)/k

Similarly, when ΔTcs reaches ΔTn at the distance ai from the interface where an active nucleant exists, nucleation occurs on the nucleant (see Fig. 3). Using ΔTn to replace ΔTcs gives(22)zn=-Dk·vln1-ΔTnQ/kwhere zn corresponds to the amount of growth when ΔTcs = ΔTn.

In most cases, ΔTn ≪ Q/k holds. Expanding the logarithmic term in Eq. (22) by neglecting the high-order terms, one obtains(23)zn≈Dv·ΔTnQwhich is identical to Eq. (16). Accordingly, it leads to the same grain size prediction as given by Eq. (17).

The two fundamentally different approaches provide a rigorous validation of the model developed. The applicability of the concept or model and its limitations in the prediction of the final grain size are discussed below.

3. Discussion

The latent dependence of the grain size on alloy variables such as ml, c0 and k has long been realized. The classical CS criterion can be written as G/V = P/D [28], where G is the temperature gradient, V is the growth velocity, D is the solute diffusion coefficient, and P=mlc0(k-1)/k=Q/k is the alloy freezing range on a binary phase diagram [42]. With this in mind, Tarshis et al. [43] performed broad survey experiments to deduce the relationship between the as-cast grain structure and alloy variables, including alloy freezing range P. The grain size was found to decrease with increasing Q/k for a wide variety of different binary nickel alloys (ten) and aluminium alloys (seven) surveyed. These experimental observations confirmed the dependence of d¯ on alloy variables in the form of Q/k or P. Then, in considering dendritic growth, Burden and Hunt [44] showed that the total undercooling at a dendrite tip increases with increasing value of mlc0(k-1). This relationship links dendritic growth and dendrite tip radius to the parameter Q [44]. The subsequent M–H model [3] considered spherical growth in undercooled alloy melts through a growth parameter S, which, similar to Eq. (12), was shown to be a function of Q. It was becoming clearer that the development of a solidifying alloy structure is related to the parameter Q. Lipton et al.’s [45] theoretical analysis of dendritic growth furthered the understanding of the influence of alloy variables in terms of Q on alloy structure evolution. They showed that the dendrite tip growth rate (dRg/dt) is proportional to 1/Q for the purely solute case, i.e., setting the thermal terms equal to zero [45]. Johnsson [19] confirmed the predicted proportional relationship between dRg/dt and 1/Q on a range of Al–Si and Al–Fe alloys. In addition, Johnsson [19] plotted the average grain size d¯ data vs 1/Q. Interestingly, they exhibited a good linear relationship. Shortly afterwards, this empirical d¯-1/Q linear relationship was further demonstrated by Chai et al. [20], Backerud and Johnsson [21] and Easton and StJohn [22] with respect to various aluminium alloys. The grain size data produced by Kearns and Cooper [46] would have shown a similar linear relationship had they plotted the data against 1/Q instead of Q/k for a significant number of aluminium alloys. Easton and StJohn [23] then investigated the empirical d¯-1/Q linear relationship on eight wrought aluminium alloys. A detailed analysis of the intercept a and the slope b of the attendant linear relationships in relation to the grain refining conditions revealed that a is related to the number of active nucleants and b to the potency of the active nucleants. More recently, the empirical linear relationship has been demonstrated on magnesium alloys [24], [26], [32] and titanium alloys [27], [28] under a variety of solidification conditions, including under ultrasonic conditions [47], [48], [49]. The linear dependence of the average grain size d¯ on 1/Q is thus an established experimental observation. This coincidentally provides support to the analytical model formulated (Eq. (17)), while at the same time the model furnishes a rigorous theoretical basis for the experimental observations for both spherical and planar growth.

Thus, the model confirms the previously realized strong relationship between grain size and Q, and also defines its slope. While the previous empirical model only predicts the relative grain size (and the actual grain size if the values of a and b are determined from experimental data), the new model is capable of predicting the actual grain size.

The system that is best studied for this verification is Al alloys inoculated with Al–Ti–B grain refiners. This is because there is detailed experimental information available about the grain refinement response to solidification conditions. The diffusivity of metal elements in liquid Al is known to be on the order of 10−9 m2 s−1 [3], [51], [52], [53], [54], [55]. Table 1 lists the calculated diffusion coefficients of the common solute/impurity elements in liquid Al at 923 K using the activation energy (Q) and pre-exponential factor (D0) data assessed by Du et al. [56]. The value of D can be taken as (3–5) × 10−9 m2 s−1 for nucleation and growth of Al grains.

The undercooling ΔTn for aluminium nucleating on TiB2 substrates is difficult to determine accurately using the current analytical means, because it is only a small fraction of one degree. Often no recalescence is observed in many measurements. One way to provide a value for ΔTn is to use the free growth model, described earlier by ΔTmin = 4γSL/(ΔSv ⋅ d) [8], [9]. The size distribution of TiB2 particles in a commercial Al–5Ti–B master alloy refiner has been analysed in detail [9]. While large particles are more effective, it has been found that the number of the TiB2 particles that are >3 μm in diameter is negligible in the master alloy. In other words, the number of these particles is too small to noticeably affect the nucleation process. The next most potent group of particles that show a good number density is those that are ∼2 μm in diameter. Accordingly, this gives an estimated undercooling of nearly 0.3 K using typical parameters (γSL = 158 × 10−3 J m−2 and ΔSv = 1.112 × 106 J K−1 m−3 [9]) for aluminium. This is reasonable, given the low undercoolings observed experimentally.

The growth velocity v can be estimated from the crystal/grain size and solidification time. While such an estimate is averaged over the whole of solidification, rather than just the beginning as required by the model, one can obtain an estimate of the order of magnitude of v for the purpose of verification of the model. For the case of grain-refined pure aluminium, the average growth velocity was found to be ∼2 μm s−1 for a pre-solidification cooling rate of 1 K s−1, given an average grain size of ∼120 μm and a solidification time, i.e., from nucleation to the end of primary solidification, of ∼60 s. The growth velocity in grain-refined aluminium alloys is expected to be similar in the early stages of solidification under analogous cooling conditions, before the effects of solute segregation and solidification temperature ranges come into play.

Given that D ≈ (3–5)×10−9 m2 s−1, ΔTn ≈ 0.3 K and v ≈ 2 × 10−6 m s−1, the slope, D ⋅ ΔTn/v, is predicted in the range 450–750 μm K, compared with 650 μm K determined from the experimental data plotted in Fig. 4. This is an excellent prediction.

The knowledge that D/v can significantly affect the grain size outcome adds to one’s ability to analyse grain size data and determine the key mechanisms controlling grain size in given alloy system and master alloy combinations. The analytical model can be used to: (i) predict the grain size for a given composition; (ii) assess any known grain refiner for improved performance; (iii) assist in defining the direction of new grain refiner development and (iv) analyse different grain refining processes. The cooling rate will most likely affect both the intercept a¯ and the slope DΔTn/vn [29]. In principle, thermal undercooling can be incorporated into the total undercooling required for nucleation as long as the cooling rate can be assessed quantitatively as a function of thermal undercooling. This will be dealt with separately in the future by superimposing a defined thermal undercooling evolution model as a function of cooling rate on the evolution of the CS.

Despite the strong support of the literature data produced under different conditions [19], [20], [21], [22], [23], [24], [26], [27], [28], [32], [47], [48], [49], it should be pointed out that the model has only dealt with the nucleation process. Nucleation plays a key role in the development of the initial structure including the size scale and spatial distribution and exerts a strong influence on the final grain size and morphology [50]. However, the final grain structure is further determined by a variety of subsequent events, including the growth of nuclei, fluid flow, grain multiplication by dendrite fragmentation and coarsening [50]. The model has not taken into account the influence of these secondary effects. A significant divergence in the model prediction may arise when such effects are not insignificant, particularly when dealing with the solidification of large castings. In theory, the analytical model formulated applies strictly to grain nucleation and formation on potent substrates where CS is predominant in relation to other forms of undercooling (i.e., thermal, curvature and interface undercooling) and the contributions of the secondary effects to the final grain density are small. Another important point to note is that the active nucleants in the model refer to those that have resulted in grain nucleation and formation. These particles may only account for a minor fraction of the nucleant particles introduced into the melt, as has been established for the inoculation of aluminium alloys with TiB2 [8], [9], [50]. The phenomenon is not yet fully understood and occurs in other systems such as ice crystallization [57], [58]. This adds another variable to the grain size prediction, as the addition level of the nucleants would seem to alter the active nucleant density available in the melt and therefore the attendant grain density to a large extent in many cases. Clearly, to predict the grain size of a solidified alloy in a comprehensive and analytical fashion remains very challenging.

4. Summary

An analytical model has been developed for CS-driven grain formation on a rigorous fundamental basis. The model links the nucleation of new grains to the growth of a larger neighbouring grain. The average grain size (d¯) is determined by two components: the minimum amount of growth (D·ΔTn/(v·Q)) that is needed to establish sufficient CS for nucleating the new grains; and the spatial mean distance (a¯) from the advancing grain front to the most potent available nucleants. Both spherical and planar growth fronts are considered covering growth fronts with curvatures from small to infinite. Two distinct fundamental approaches are used to formulate the grain formation, with both approaches resulting in identical descriptions of d¯, where d¯=a¯+D·ΔTn/(v·Q) (D is the solute diffusion coefficient, ΔTn is the undercooling for nucleation, v is the growth velocity, and Q is the growth restriction factor, Q=mlc0(k-1)). The two approaches provide validation of the model under the assumptions used. In addition, the model confirms a strong empirical linear relationship between grain size and 1/Q that has been previously recognized and is able to give reasonable predictions of the grain size variation with Q, given estimates of the input parameters.
